topic: AI Ontology Failures and Structural Hallucination (2025-2026 Frontier Research)

findings.title: Why LLMs Hallucinate on Structured Knowledge: A Mechanistic Analysis of Reasoning over Linearized Representations
findings.key_findings: Introduces Structural Shortcut Reliance (SSR) and Semantic Alignment Score (SAS) as mechanistic diagnostic metrics. SSR quantifies concentration of attention on structural regularities in linearized inputs via attention heads. SAS employs FFNs to evaluate alignment between internal representations and supporting evidence during generation. Combined SSR+SAS achieves AUC 0.8328-0.8506 for hallucination detection across LLaMA2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, substantially outperforming either metric alone (SSR-only AUC ~0.55, SAS-only AUC ~0.63). Establishes that hallucinations on structured knowledge arise from over-reliance on structural heuristics rather than semantic evidence.

findings.title: When Do Hallucinations Arise? A Graph Perspective on the Evolution of Path Reuse and Path Compression
findings.key_findings: Formalizes two core mechanisms underlying reasoning hallucinations in decoder-only Transformers: Path Reuse and Path Compression. Path Reuse arises in early training when the model learns underlying graph structure before contextual constraints, causing it to default to high-traffic memorized paths even when prompts explicitly exclude them. Path Compression emerges in later training as frequently traversed multi-step paths collapse into shortcut edges, causing accuracy to decline after initial improvement. Path compression predominantly occurs when reasoning transitions skip low-out-degree bridge nodes and directly jump to high-out-degree nodes, bypassing community-level structure.

findings.title: Structural Hallucination in Large Language Models: A Network-Based Evaluation of Knowledge Organization and Citation Integrity
findings.key_findings: Introduces the concept of structural hallucination as a distinct failure mode where individually plausible statements collectively misrepresent the relational architecture of a knowledge domain. Evaluates LLMs on three benchmarks: biographical knowledge organization, citation network reconstruction, and bibliographic metadata. Hallucination rates exceed 93% in structured biographical fields and approach 100% for DOI reconstruction. Dominant error mode is fabrication (generating plausible but unsupported content) rather than omission. Two failure modes identified: Fabrication/Confabulation and Relational Non-Retrievability.

findings.title: KGHaluBench: A Knowledge Graph-Based Hallucination Benchmark for Evaluating the Breadth and Depth of LLM Knowledge
findings.key_findings: Presents KGHaluBench, a comprehensive KG-based hallucination benchmark that dynamically generates multifaceted compound questions from randomly selected entities in knowledge graphs. Evaluates 25 frontier LLMs using novel accuracy and hallucination metrics. Automated verification pipeline detects abstentions and verifies responses at both conceptual and correctness levels. Key finding: primary frontier for LLM development is not just recognizing more entities, but improving precision of detailed factual recall. Addresses popularity bias through statistical difficulty estimation.

findings.title: When structure predicts hallucination: Aligning LLMs with knowledge graph features
findings.key_findings: Investigates correlation between entropy-based KG features and LLM response accuracy. Entropy features capture diversity and uncertainty within structured knowledge, identifying 'blind spots' where LLMs are prone to hallucination. Entropy-guided probing effectively targets cases of factual error, proving more challenging for LLMs overall. Demonstrates that structured features from KGs can predict hallucination susceptibility, providing insights for building more reliable AI systems.

findings.title: OAEI-LLM-T: A TBox Benchmark Dataset for Understanding Large Language Model Hallucinations in Ontology Matching
findings.key_findings: Extends the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) TBox datasets with LLM-specific hallucination annotations across 10 different LLMs performing ontology matching tasks. Analyzes named classes and properties within ontology pairs. Schema extends EDOAL and SSSSOM standards with hallucination tags capturing entities involved, similarity measures, relations, and confidence levels. Captures hallucination typology specific to schema matching tasks, enabling systematic study of when and how LLMs hallucinate on structured ontological knowledge.

findings.title: Reasoning Path Compression: Compressing Generation Trajectories for Efficient LLM Reasoning
findings.key_findings: Introduces RPC, a training-free method for accelerating inference of reasoning language models by leveraging semantic sparsity in reasoning paths. Improves throughput and reduces memory usage with minimal accuracy drop through semantic-aware pruning that retains only high-importance tokens. While focused on efficiency, provides diagnostic insights into which path segments are essential versus redundant in reasoning trajectories, with implications for understanding path compression failures.

findings.title: A Geometric Taxonomy of Hallucinations in Large Language Models
findings.key_findings: Extends the Semantic Grounding Index (SGI) geometric framework to context-free settings. Demonstrates that different hallucination types have fundamentally different geometric signatures in embedding space. Uses angular ratio measurement on unit hypersphere to detect unfaithfulness, achieving large effect sizes (Cohen's d up to 1.28). Consistency validated across multiple embedding architectures (sentence-t5-large, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2, bge-base, e5-base). Establishes spherical triangle inequality as predictive of detection performance.

findings.title: An Ontology of LLM Failure Modes
findings.key_findings: Synthesizes findings from approximately 25 academic papers and industry publications (2024-2026) into comprehensive taxonomy. Incorporates ErrorAtlas (catalogued error patterns across 8,383 models with 17 top-level categories), OWASP LLM Top 10:2025, Geometric Taxonomy of Hallucinations, and Microsoft's Agentic AI Failure Taxonomy. Result: eight top-level categories containing over 60 distinct failure modes. Provides structured framework for diagnosing ontology-related failures alongside other LLM failure types.

findings.title: Language Without Propositions: Why Large Language Models Hallucinate
findings.key_findings: Philosophical analysis arguing that LLMs lack adequate representation of propositions due to a combination of technical and philosophical reasons. Links hallucination to the traditional tension between coherence and correspondence theories of truth: LLM outputs may simulate truth through textual coherence but remain epistemically suspended without external grounding. Identifies that LLM makeup is based on an implicit account of language that does not give sufficient weight to propositions. Their textual coherence may simulate truth but without external grounding, outputs remain plausible yet unanchored in reality.

findings.title: Epistemic Limits of Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models
findings.key_findings: Integrates philosophical analysis with empirical developments in LLM design to clarify epistemological implications of hallucination. Examines fundamental limits of what can be achieved through technical mitigation strategies alone. Contributes to understanding why hallucinations persist despite advances in retrieval augmentation, alignment, and verification methods.

findings.title: Rethinking Error: 'Hallucinations' and Epistemological Indifference
findings.key_findings: Argues hallucinations are not errors in the conventional sense but evidence of a probabilistic system incapable of dealing with questions of knowledge. Characterizes LLMs as 'epistemologically indifferent'—they generate outputs without regard for truth. Urges viewing hallucinations as practical reminders of the limits of this kind of machine learning rather than as fixable bugs. Challenges the assumption that hallucinations will be swept away as technology improves.

findings.title: Hallucination Detection in Long-Form Text Generated by LLMs: A Benchmark and a Hyper-Relational Knowledge Graph Approach
findings.key_findings: Addresses limitations of prior benchmarks focused on short-form content by introducing long-form hallucination detection benchmark. Proposes hyper-relational KG approach that captures long-range and hyper-relational dependencies beyond coarse-grained consistency checks. Demonstrates that structural complexity of long-form scenarios requires more sophisticated detection methods than those sufficient for short-form content.

findings.title: Beyond Predefined Schemas: TRACE-KG for Context-Enriched Knowledge Graph Generation
findings.key_findings: Presents TRACE-KG for context-enriched KG generation from complex documents without predefined schemas. Uses topology-aware evaluation with schema element retrieval (top-K=5 per anchor), LLM verifier for alignment, anchored matching threshold, and human audit for low-confidence outputs. Demonstrates schema-adaptive KG construction that reduces hallucination through structural constraints while maintaining flexibility.

findings.title: Why Language Models Hallucinate
findings.key_findings: Argues that language models hallucinate because standard training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty. Most benchmarks measure accuracy in ways that encourage confident answers rather than honest uncertainty expression. On simple evaluations models can achieve near 100% accuracy, but on challenging evaluations accuracy is capped below 100% due to unavailable information or inherent ambiguity. Proposes that evaluation reform is necessary to incentivize appropriate abstention.

summary: Research in 2025-2026 has produced significant advances in understanding LLM hallucinations on structured knowledge through multiple complementary lenses. Mechanistically, SSR and SAS metrics demonstrate that hallucinations arise from over-reliance on structural heuristics (attention concentration on regularities) rather than semantic evidence alignment (FFN-based grounding). Graph-theoretic analyses reveal two fundamental failure mechanisms: Path Reuse (early training memorization overriding contextual constraints) and Path Compression (later training collapse of multi-step reasoning into shortcuts). The KGHaluBench benchmark provides the first KG-grounded evaluation decomposing hallucinations into breadth and depth components across 25+ LLMs, while OAEI-LLM-T extends ontology matching benchmarks with hallucination typologies. Structural hallucination is now recognized as a distinct failure mode where individually correct statements collectively misrepresent relational architecture, with fabrication rates exceeding 93-100% in structured tasks. Entropy-based KG features can predict hallucination susceptibility by identifying knowledge 'blind spots.' Philosophically, analyses frame hallucinations as inevitable consequences of LLMs' lack of propositional representation and epistemological indifference—systems that generate plausible text without truth-grounding. The emerging consensus: hallucinations are not fixable bugs but structural properties of probabilistic generation requiring layered mitigation (RAG, guardrails, verification gates, structural constraints) rather than complete elimination.
